nameStory: The American lobster gets its name from its home range along the American Atlantic coast, distinguishing it from its European cousin. You'll also hear it called Maine lobster since Maine's cold waters produce some of the finest specimens, though these crustaceans actually range from Canada down to New Jersey.
description: The American lobster is a massive marine crustacean that looks like an underwater armored knight with two unequal claws and a segmented tail. These impressive creatures typically appear bluish-green to brown with reddish spines, though rare color variations like blue, yellow, or even split-colored lobsters occasionally turn up. They can grow to truly impressive sizes - up to 25 inches long and weighing over 44 pounds, making them the heaviest crustaceans in the world. Their bodies are covered in a hard shell called an exoskeleton that they must shed periodically as they grow.

idTips.label: Unequal Claws
idTips.description: One claw is noticeably larger and heavier with blunt teeth for crushing, while the other is smaller and more slender with sharp edges for cutting - like having a hammer and scissors

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Living lobsters are typically mottled bluish-green to dark brown with bright red or orange spines scattered across the shell, not the bright red color you see after cooking

idTips.label: Rostrum Spines
idTips.description: The pointed beak-like projection between the eyes has sharp spines on both top and bottom sides that feel like thorns when touched carefully

idTips.label: Segmented Tail
idTips.description: The muscular tail fan has distinct segments that feel firm and flexible, capable of powerful backward propulsion when threatened

idTips.label: Long Antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of antennae extend from the head - the longer pair can be nearly as long as the body and feel smooth and whip-like

idTips.label: Walking Legs
idTips.description: Four pairs of jointed walking legs beneath the body, with the shell feeling rough and bumpy to the touch, covered in small spines and tubercles

habitat: American lobsters live on rocky, sandy, and muddy bottoms along New England's coast from the intertidal zone down to depths of several hundred feet. They prefer areas with plenty of crevices, caves, and rocky ledges where they can hide during the day, often sharing these underwater neighborhoods with sea urchins, crabs, and various fish species. You're most likely to encounter them in lobster traps, tide pools, or while scuba diving along the rocky Maine coast.

seasonality.spring: Lobsters begin moving into shallower waters as temperatures warm, making this prime time for coastal sightings in tide pools and shallow rocky areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak lobster season when they're most active and closer to shore, with the best chance of spotting them in deeper tide pools or during diving excursions.
seasonality.fall: Still active in coastal waters but beginning to move to deeper areas as water temperatures drop, though still catchable in traditional lobster grounds.
seasonality.winter: Lobsters retreat to deeper, warmer waters offshore and become less active, making encounters rare except in deeper fishing operations.

funFact: Lobsters are practically immortal - they don't age the way most animals do and can theoretically live forever if they avoid predators, disease, and fishing traps, with some specimens estimated to be over 100 years old!
confusionNotes: In New England waters, American lobsters are unlikely to be confused with anything else due to their distinctive large claws and size, though small juveniles might be mistaken for crayfish - but crayfish live in freshwater while lobsters are strictly marine.
contextualKnowledge: Many people think lobsters are naturally bright red, but that's only the color they turn when cooked - living lobsters are actually quite well-camouflaged in mottled greens and browns. The lobster industry is deeply woven into New England culture and economy, particularly in Maine where lobster boats with their colorful buoys are as much a part of the landscape as lighthouses.
compareHints: The American lobster is the only true lobster species in New England waters, making it unique among local crustaceans. Its closest relative is the European lobster found across the Atlantic, which can be distinguished by its different coloration pattern and lack of spines on the underside of the rostrum (the pointed beak between the eyes). Unlike spiny lobsters found in warmer waters, American lobsters have those distinctive large claws that spiny lobsters completely lack.
